story_text.value:
I paid $19 for Kimi Code to test K3.1 Pro Standard (not Highspeed) using the official CLI v2.3.1.

I ran two tasks on small repositories:

1. Recommend movies based on an existing movie database. 2. Analyze a website's codebase.

Neither task completed. The entire 5-hour quota was exhausted within minutes.

I analyzed the actual session logs, including background agents:

- Fresh input: 368,203 tokens - Cached input: 1,183,744 tokens - Output: 39,324 tokens - Total: 1.59M tokens

At Kimi's published API rates, that's just $1.37 worth of usage before hitting the 5-hour limit which is easily less than 5% of what Claude Code offers at $20 subscription.

The logs show: "429 You've reached your 5-hour usage limit."

For comparison, Claude Code on a $20 subscription processed roughly 381M tokens over 4-5 hours using Opus 5.5 xhigh, mostly cached input. That's not a controlled benchmark, but the difference in usable capacity is staggering.

Both Kimi tasks failed without delivering results. I have video evidence and detailed logs, but won't publish private repository data.

Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hSr-DLn88AM

Is this a quota-accounting bug, or are Kimi's $19 subscription limits intentionally this restrictive?

Disclosure: I also develop a competing coding agent. These tests used Kimi's official CLI.

title.value: Ask HN: Kimi Code hit its 5-hour limit after $1.37 of API usage

story_text.value:
The fastest way to learn harness engineering? Build Claude Code from scratch.

Why harness engineering? LangChain kept the same model and changed only the harness. Their coding agent went from 53% to 67% on Terminal-Bench, a top coding-agent benchmark. From outside the top 30 to the top 5. Same model. Better harness.

Over the past few months, I've taken apart Claude Code, OpenCode, and Pi to see how they work under the hood.

And you don't need to ship a coding agent for this to pay off. The same foundations power any agent, in e-commerce, finance, or sales.

On top of that, people are increasingly realizing they need to build their own harness instead of relying on Claude Code or Codex. Ramp scaling its operations with a custom harness is a perfect example.

So I turned what I learned into an in-depth course on harness engineering by building Claude Code from scratch. It's free and open source: 8 articles, 6 videos, and one codebase. It's perfect for people who learn by building. Everything in Python.

For full transparency, Modal, Opik, and Kitaru sponsor the course, which lets me keep it 100% free as an independent AI engineer.

Here are the 8 steps that I think are core to building and maintaining any harness:

1. Design the harness 2. Build the bare-bones agent loop 3. Sandbox it, locally and remotely 4. Apply 4 essential context engineering techniques 5. Add subagents as a context engineering technique 6. Deploy it headless to the cloud: CLI, webhooks, cron 7. Build benchmarks to measure it 8. Replay failed runs to debug agents

Everything is on GitHub: https://github.com/decodingai-magazine/building-a-coding-agent-from-scratch-course

Curious what others here think. Which of these steps has been the hardest to get right in your own agents?

title.value: Took apart Claude Code, then turned it into a free course on harness engineering

story_text.value:
I'm building Multipeer, a desktop app for running agents, tools and working wth teammates on one shared canvas.

I often have several agent sessions open at once, but they're all scattered across terminals. It was also hard for my co-founder to see what my agents are doing or jump in to work together. So We built the solution to our own problem. And now we're releasing it to the world.

It's a macOS app for now (soon on Windows and Linux). You can invite your teammates over a local network or over the internet. They can follow your view and, if you allow them, they can also take control of your terminal and claude code/codex sessions.

The app is still early, and I'm also releasing the iPhone/Android app soon to remotely control everything on your canvas.

I'd would like to get feedback from the HN community! If there's any features you'd like to see, please contact me via: shyam@multipeer.sh, we build really fast. I'd love to talk to everyone of you and work on your feedback!

Thanks!

Hope this helps and thanks for your time!

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Faithful. I built dánwò, an open-source (Apache-2.0) end-to-end testing framework for web and mobile apps, written in TypeScript.

The problem: a UI test can click "Pay", see "Payment successful" and pass, while the card was charged twice, the webhook was handled twice, or the receipt email never went out. With coding agents writing more of our code, that gap between "the screen looks right" and "the right things happened" is where I kept finding bugs.

How it works:

- Tests drive the app like a user, with locators or plain-English agent steps. An agent step calls a model once; danwo records the actions and replays them on later runs with no model calls, so CI doesn't need an API key.

- Your app runs behind an egress proxy. Calls to Stripe, Clerk, Resend, Slack, Google and about 20 other providers are answered by local emulators at the real hostnames, so there are no sandbox keys and no code changes. For Node apps a preload routes the calls; Bun honours HTTPS_PROXY.

- An invariant is a check that runs after the test and compares two sides: what the provider says happened (charges, emails, messages) and what your app stored. For example, credits granted must equal paid checkouts times 500.

- `danwo matrix` replays a test once per fault it could meet: a 500 or 429 from a provider, a declined card, a duplicate, late, forged or replayed webhook, a double-submit, a database commit whose reply is lost, Postgres unreachable for a few seconds. The invariant judges every run, so you see exactly which failure your app mishandles.

- Every run leaves a flight record: video, each step, every provider call, webhook delivery and database statement, with secrets redacted.

It runs in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, and on the Android emulator and iOS Simulator. It ships an MCP server and a skill, so coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) can write and run tests and fix what fails.

Limitations, honestly: the emulators are only as good as their fidelity to the real APIs. Each one has a suite that runs against the real provider to catch drift, but they won't cover every edge of Stripe's API. Backend routing is built for Node and Bun today. Mobile tests need macOS or Linux. It's early (v0.1.2).

The name is Yorùbá: "dán an wò" means "try it and see".

Quickstart: npx @danwo/cli init (docs: https://danwo.dev/docs/quickstart)

I'd love feedback, especially on faults you've been bitten by that aren't in the matrix yet.

title.value: Show HN: Dánwò – Open-source E2E testing with emulators and fault injection

story_text.value:
Hey everyone,

Inspired by Herdr, I've built an agent multiplexer that I've been using as my daily driver for a few weeks now.

I think I improved on the concept in a few ways, focusing on the ergonomics I always wished I had:

I show you what the agents are up to, along with a running feed of their activity. There's also a simple shortcut (F1) to go to the next unread agent.

I use multiple accounts, so I've added unified launcher for Codex/Claude Code/Pi. Theres some careful ergonomics there: fast search and resume over sessions, inline usage tracking etc.

Many small quality of life improvements to the terminal experience: - Links can be copied with a click, so no need to drag-select over many lines - cmd+v just pastes images (even on SSH) - images have a thumbnail preview. - Built-in CPU/Memory/GPU usage tracking, broken down by workspace

I assume you have access to cheap inference (Luna/Haiku/etc). It just reuses the agents to organize things for you: what is this http link? what is this worktree about? what is each agent doing? It's small but it made my environment feel more cozy.

On a personal note, I've been on a frustrating sick leave for a while now. I created Corgi to challenge myself, and see if I can go back. The answer is more mixed than I had hoped, but I am happy with the result and thankful for the experience.

I hope you like it! a few friends & myself have been using it for a few weeks and it's been pretty nice. There's still a lot to improve and some rough edges, so feedback would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you :)

title.value: Show HN: Corgi, a helpful {agent, terminal} multiplexer

story_text.value:
A few years ago when Stable Diffusion was released, I happened to be reading Homer's Iliad and came across a section where Achilles' shield is described in great detail. I fed the passage into Stable Diffusion, wondering how well it would do in creating an illustration of the shield. Of course it was terrible, but a year later DALL-E 3 seemed to do a pretty good job, as long as you didn't look too hard at the details. By then I had been reading Gibbon's Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire (yes I had been on a classics binge), and created a Python app that let me feed random paragraphs into DALL-E 3. The results were often grand collages that seemed to look like a combination of Renaissance art and graffiti.

After playing around with this idea for a bit, I realized it would be pretty cool to have a dedicated app that could download public-domain books and illustrate them with DALL-E 3. I have been working on this idea for a few years, at first copying code back and forth from Xcode to the ChatGPT prompt, and then later using Claude Code. I didn't know anything about developing for the iPhone, and had to tackle a broad range of issues, everything from setting up a serverless backend to writing code in Swift to releasing an app on the App Store. Technical issues as mundane as how to parse an EPUB correctly or how to create an engaging UI/UX were surprisingly complex.

Now this work has finally culminated in an app I call ParaGraFX: a free-to-download EPUB book reader with built-in text-to-image generation. This app is designed to make public-domain books easy to download and illustrate, with download tools for Project Gutenberg, Standard Ebooks, and The Internet Archive, and illustrations powered by fal.ai and OpenAI.

To get started just download the app and open one of the bundled books to start reading. At the bottom of the screen is a button labeled 'Illustrate', which can create an illustration based on selected text or the text on screen. Are you reading the section in Alice in Wonderland about the Mad Hatter's tea party? Just hit 'Illustrate' and you will be served with a custom illustration in one of three dozen styles — from Romantic oil painting, Japanese woodblock print and Art Deco poster to Byzantine mosaic, a cross-stitch sampler, 16-bit pixel art, or 1980s teletext block graphics. You can modify the generated illustration by either editing the original prompt, or providing custom instructions, such as adding the Queen of Hearts in the background.

This app is free to download and use for reading EPUBs, but since images cost money to generate, they are paid for with credits. The first 3 credits are free, and additional credits are available for purchase starting at $1.99 for 10 credits. There are 4 tiers of image quality that cost different numbers of credits, with the Fast tier costing 1 credit per image, and 5 credits for the Best tier, which uses OpenAI's top image model. (The free 3 credits are restricted to the Fast tier.)

I invite you to try it out and give me feedback in the comments. Whether you want to use it as a serious reader, or want to surf from book to book just to create illustrations, ParaGraFX grew out of the simple pleasure of illustrating the classics.

title.value: Show HN: ParaGraFX – An iOS app for reading and illustrating ePub books

story_text.value:
Hey Everyone, After getting frustrated by Claude rewriting key functions and still making the test pass, was tinkering around with a review tool, that would track the assumptions and decisions the agent took, without me digging through the entire session. So ended up building Sonah. Sonah is basically a code reviewer that not only reads the code and diff but also the agent session that wrote the code, to understand the assumptions, and decisions your agent took along the way. And highlight important parts of the code that need your attention.

Sonah uses your existing claude code/codex subscription (claude preferred for higher context window). You can try using below: npm install -g getsonah sonah doctor cd your-project && sonah review --format html --output ~/review.html

title.value: Show HN: Sonah, code reviewer that reads your agent's session, not only the diff

story_text.value:
I have a question, and I hope you can clarify it. Consider this scenario: Claude code runs on a desktop to develop a solution, and its directive requires Codex to test everything it does under a different directive. The Codex directive is to refute Claude's test results, maintain its own test ledger, and return PASS or NO PASS. Claude cannot negotiate; it has to fix the NO PASS issues. Even with such a strict environment, I am ending up with problems, and of course, when asking Claude, the answer is "This is on me; I did not do X and Y"; when I ask it whether Codex checked it, "Codex checked all but not this "...

So when can we trust the AI to do the full job, not just the happy path? Is there a better way to impose quality?

I feel that on large projects, even if I upload Claude directives to re-read, Claude or Codex (we can switch roles) tends to drift and miss things.

title.value: Ask HN: When can we trust AI in coding, and avoid the happy path issue?

The Codex directive is to refute Claude's test results, maintain its own test ledger, and return PASS or NO PASS. Claude cannot negotiate; it has to fix the NO PASS issues. Even with such a strict environment, I am ending up with problems, and of course, when asking Claude, the answer is "This is on me; I did not do X and Y"; when I ask it whether Codex checked it, "Codex checked all but not this "...

So when can we trust the AI to do the full job, not just the happy path? Is there a better way to impose quality?

I feel that on large projects, even if I upload Claude directives to re-read, Claude or Codex (we can switch roles) tends to drift and miss things.

story_text.value:
I know there are many dictation apps out there, but I built one myself anyways based on my custom needs. Since OpenAI dictation is so good, my previous workflow would be speaking to ChatGPT UI and pasting a default prompt to turn my speech into a well formatted prompt

Now I just hold a key (Fn for me), talk, let go, and the text gets pasted wherever the cursor is, mostly Claude Code in the terminal. The default prompt part became "Modes" where you write the instructions once (clean it up, translate to English, etc) and the transcript goes through an OpenAI model before it's pasted.

It uses your own OpenAI key and calls their API directly, no server in between. My daily spend is usually around US$ 0.15.

It's cloud only, so if you want local models Handy or VoiceInk are better picks. No signed release yet, you build it with Xcode using one script. MIT licensed.

story_text.value:
One day while I was sitting working on a personal project I was building using Claude Code I decided to give it a prompt about how I want it to build a function for me that would be directly connected to my database, well did I know that I would be shocked with what actually happened. When I started working on this project of mine, I had decided that I would want to use PostgreSQL purely because I felt that it is the one to use as I did not know a lot about the different databases. Soon after I decided that after doing some research it makes a lot of sense to use MySQL for this project and I discussed this with ChatGPT and I changed my database completely and was working with a MySQL database. To my surprise, the AI models did not realize that, once I got back on Claude and was trying to design a future function something looked not so right to me and there it was - functions were written in a way that I was still using PostgreSQL and they were not at all written in a way for MySQL so it was not possible for them to work and Claude was writing them with so much confidence as in its memory it remembered it as a PostgreSQL.

I was shocked and bamboozled by this honestly so I decided to test it on Cursor and see if it is a thing where the AI model’s memory does not get updated the way it should. That was the moment I decided that I should make Mnemolith, for as insane the name sounds it actually means memory stone and for some reason I thought of carvings on stones as a memory and in this scenario we can change these carvings and basically keep our memory updating. I started building Mnemolith and now I can proudly say that it works on your own local computer (hopefully no bugs but if you find any bugs or anything that I should improve on, please let me know) and is connected to your AI agents like Cursor, Claude Code and Codex. Now memories that are linked to your project files get flagged as soon as those files change, and the user will also find out what happened and they can decide if they want to rewrite what was saved or if it was something that can be ignored. Setup tells the AI models to call Mnemolith, and we let them know which memories changed or were replaced and why, so that they don’t build on old facts and we save time. In our system, each memory stores a hash of the files it depends on so even before a commit we are able to find what changes and the best part is that this all started as a codecrafter’s challenge on building your own redis using java. I would love to know what your AI keeps getting wrong about your projects and any feedback regarding this and things I should work on in the future.
